data.hypothesis: The previously measured lane-state kernel seeds from a full first vector and uses scalar handling for short inputs and the tail. Initializing each lane to the sentinel tuple (INT_MAX, INT_MAX), processing every full vector, and using one masked final vector should remove those special paths while preserving signed value-first, earliest-index ordering, including INT32_MAX. The per-vector tuple comparisons add work, so this tests whether simpler boundary handling offsets that cost; no speedup is assumed.

memory_lessons.applicability: The recorded timings and correctness cases used one thread and n=8192; they do not establish performance across sizes or patterns.
memory_lessons.claim: The earlier AVX-512 lane-state implementation was correct on five recorded correctness patterns and measured a mean of about 0.990 microseconds, versus the baseline mean of about 4.463 microseconds. These observations motivate testing a contrasting boundary and tuple-update strategy, but do not predict its result.
memory_lessons.next_experiment: Have the controller validate this masked-tail, sentinel-initialized variant and compare its repeated timings under the same frozen protocol.

data.notes: This is a contrasting implementation to the recorded seeded-first-vector/scalar-tail candidate. The supplied target is EPYC 9654 with GCC 14.2 and one thread; the earlier AVX-512 candidate was valid and measured faster than the baseline. This proposal has not been measured or validated; the controller should perform correctness checks and repeated timings, including extrema and ties.
transformations: Initialize 16 signed lane minima and their earliest-index state with the sentinel tuple (INT_MAX, INT_MAX), then process all complete 16-element vectors.
Update per-lane state using signed value-first and index-second tuple ordering, including equality with INT_MAX when the lane is still at its sentinel state.
Replace the scalar short-input path and scalar tail with a masked final vector, then reduce lane results by value and index; return index zero for non-positive n.
